rows.source: HSE workplace-radon guidance
rows.verified: Radon is a radioactive gas that cannot be seen, smelled or tasted and requires measurement equipment for detection.

rows.source: HSE workplace-radon guidance
rows.verified: Radon can accumulate in many types of workplace and is an important cause of lung cancer.

rows.source: HSE workplace-radon guidance
rows.verified: Employers must review the potential radon hazard in their premises.

rows.source: HSE workplace-radon guidance
rows.verified: Above-ground workplaces in radon-affected areas should normally include measurements in appropriate ground-floor rooms.

rows.source: HSE workplace-radon guidance
rows.verified: Occupied below-ground workplaces should include radon measurements irrespective of the above-ground affected-area status.

rows.source: HSE workplace-radon guidance
rows.verified: All indoor workplace types can have high radon levels depending on location, structure and use.

rows.source: HSE workplace-radon guidance
rows.verified: Where the annual average concentration is at or above 300 Bq per cubic metre, IRR17 applies and HSE notification is required.

rows.source: HSE workplace-radon guidance
rows.verified: Control measures and occupancy restrictions must be verified by remeasurement, with review frequency reflecting the measured level and effectiveness of remediation.

rows.source: HSE workplace-radon guidance
rows.verified: Radon risk depends on geology, building location and structure, floor level, ventilation, occupancy, measurement duration, seasonal variation and remediation performance.

rows.source: HSE workplace-radon guidance
rows.verified: General radon risk assessment, measurement, notification, remediation and review guidance does not prove current conditions or control performance at an individual parcel and does not establish an exact incident, exposure or illness probability.

rows.source: HSE artificial and natural optical-radiation guidance
rows.verified: Optical radiation includes ultraviolet radiation, visible light and infrared radiation.

rows.source: HSE artificial and natural optical-radiation guidance
rows.verified: Ultraviolet exposure can damage the eyes and skin and can contribute to skin cancer.

rows.source: HSE artificial and natural optical-radiation guidance
rows.verified: High-power lasers can cause serious eye injury, including blindness, and can burn skin.

rows.source: HSE artificial and natural optical-radiation guidance
rows.verified: The Control of Artificial Optical Radiation at Work Regulations protect workers from hazardous artificial optical-radiation sources.

rows.source: HSE artificial and natural optical-radiation guidance
rows.verified: Employers should identify hazardous sources and assess whether existing controls reduce exposure sufficiently.

rows.source: HSE artificial and natural optical-radiation guidance
rows.verified: Where hazardous artificial optical-radiation risks remain, exposure should be reduced as low as reasonably practicable.

rows.source: HSE artificial and natural optical-radiation guidance
rows.verified: Risk controls may include enclosure, interlocks, screens, restricted access, safe operating procedures, training and suitable eye or skin protection.

rows.source: HSE artificial and natural optical-radiation guidance
rows.verified: Natural sunlight, sunbeds, lasers and other sources require source-specific controls rather than assuming all optical radiation presents the same risk.

rows.source: HSE artificial and natural optical-radiation guidance
rows.verified: Optical-radiation risk depends on wavelength, source power, beam geometry, exposure duration and distance, reflections, shielding, skin and eye protection and worker sensitivity.

rows.source: HSE artificial and natural optical-radiation guidance
rows.verified: General assessment and control of ultraviolet, visible, infrared and laser radiation guidance does not prove current conditions or control performance at an individual parcel and does not establish an exact incident, exposure or illness probability.
